intro: Read the deck for the arguments and these notes for the working-out. Each note explains a slide, gives you a way to remember it and warns where researchers slip. Try the section exercises on a study of your own, answer the recall questions aloud, and write your positionality paragraph beside mine as you go.

sections.title: What Feminist Research Is
sections.big_idea: Feminist research is **a stance on knowledge and power**. It applies to any topic and adds a second set of questions to the usual ones.
in_plain_words: Many people think feminist research means studying women or adding a gender variable. It is a way of doing research that treats knowledge as shaped by power, especially gendered power, and works to surface and shift that power. You can study irrigation, fiscal transfers or migration this way. The test is whether the framing of the question changed.

It keeps ordinary standards of evidence and adds questions: true for whom, whose question is this, who is missing, who benefits. Knowledge is made through five decisions: the question, the evidence, who is asked, how answers are coded and what is published. **Documenting those five choices** is the minimal practical form of the whole argument.

left.title: What it is often taken for
items: A variable added to a model

right.title: What it is
items: A stance on knowledge and power
A question about who set the model
A way of doing any study

key_terms.meaning: Inquiry that treats knowledge as shaped by power and works to surface and shift it.
A description of research choices as consequential; it gives no licence to pick findings.
One of five choices that make a fact: question, evidence, sample, coding, publication.
Who decides what is worth studying; often funder and researcher.
A definition such as 'poor' or 'work' that decides who the state sees.
A feminist lens that changed only the analysis and left the framing alone.

worked_example.title: Was the lens applied at the right stage?
worked_example.setup: A funder tells a team to 'add a feminist lens' to a study of irrigation scheme uptake. The team adds a sex-disaggregation table.
steps: Ask the slide's test: did the framing of the research question change?
The question is still 'what share of households adopt the scheme?' Only the analysis changed.
So the lens was applied at the wrong stage.
Revisit the five decision points: who set the question, what counts as evidence, who is asked, how answers are coded, what is published.
Reframe: ask who decides the scheme's eligibility and whose water use counts as use.
worked_example.answer: The lens arrived too late. Reframing the question itself, beyond adding a table, is what makes it feminist.

mistakes: Equating feminist research with research about women or a sex-disaggregation table.
Treating every qualitative study as feminist, or every statistical study as outside it.
Reading 'political act' as permission to choose findings politically.
Listing a category or definition as a technical decision when it works as an allocation decision.

recall.q: What is the slide's test for whether a feminist lens has been applied?
recall.a: Whether the framing of the research question changed.

recall.q: Name the five decision points that make a fact.
recall.a: Which question is asked, what counts as evidence, who is asked, how answers are coded and what is published.

recall.q: What does feminist research ask in addition to 'what is true?'
recall.a: True for whom, told by whom, in whose interest.

recall.q: Which misreading does Harding's argument answer?
recall.a: That feminist research abandons objectivity; Harding argues mainstream objectivity is too weak.

recall.q: What should you ask when a number moves after a definition changes?
recall.a: Whether the world changed or the category did.

sections.title: A Short History
sections.big_idea: Feminist research began as a **critique of 'objective' science** and grew into three live positions, with a South Asian tradition alongside.
in_plain_words: The critique began with documented cases, such as medical research on men generalised to everyone. If the knowers were so partial, how could the knowledge be universal? The waves of feminism are a rough Western map. For research the second wave mattered most, because 'the personal is political' made housework, care and domestic violence worthy objects of study.

Sandra Harding distinguished three responses: feminist empiricism, standpoint theory and postmodern feminism. They are live positions you choose between, with no ladder to climb. South Asian scholarship on caste and patriarchy, the household and invisible labour developed in parallel. **Cite it as theory in its own right**, and keep case material for the data.

children.label: Standpoint theory
items: Position shapes what can be known

key_terms.meaning: Treats sexist bias as bad science, correctable by more careful, inclusive work.
Argues the margins can see more of how a system works.
Distrusts universal truths, stressing 'woman' is not one thing.
Second-wave insight that private life is structured by public power.
Centred on men's experience.
The risk that no account can be preferred to another.

worked_example.title: Which position is being used?
worked_example.setup: Three researchers each respond to a clinical trial that enrolled only men.
steps: A says: include women and check the instrument for bias. That is feminist empiricism, which fixes bias inside existing rules.
B says: start from the lives of women patients, since position shapes what can be known. That is standpoint theory.
C says: no single account of 'women's health' is complete, so we need several partial accounts. That is postmodern feminism.
Note the cost of each: empiricism leaves neutral method largely unquestioned, and postmodernism risks relativism.
worked_example.answer: A is empiricism, B is standpoint theory, C is postmodern feminism.

mistakes: Treating the three positions as stages a researcher passes through.
Using the waves as gospel for South Asia, where feminisms followed their own timelines.
Citing South Asian scholarship only as context.
Reading postmodern humility as permission for relativism.

recall.q: Which wave does the deck call decisive for research?
recall.a: The second wave.

recall.q: What is the limit of feminist empiricism?
recall.a: It cannot see bias built into the standards themselves.

recall.q: What is a standpoint, in Harding's sense?
recall.a: An analytical achievement won through struggle and reflection; group membership alone does not confer it.

recall.q: What risk does postmodern feminism carry?
recall.a: A relativism that can dissolve the political ground feminism needs.

recall.q: Name two South Asian questions that Western frameworks handled badly.
recall.a: Any two of: caste and patriarchy together, the household as a site of inequality, women's invisible labour, personal law and religion.

sections.title: Core Commitments
sections.big_idea: Five commitments recur: **reflexivity, positionality, power, voice and reciprocity**. They are practice, and each has a one-line test.
in_plain_words: Positionality names where you stand: gender, caste, class, language, institution. Reflexivity examines how your identity, assumptions and presence shape every stage. Power runs through the research relationship, and participants hold levers too, including silence and the power to refuse. Voice means carrying people's words faithfully without claiming to give voice. Reciprocity means something flows back.

The commitments reinforce one another: naming your position makes reflexivity possible, which reveals power, which you act on through voice and reciprocity. **They only mean something if they change what you do.** A positionality paragraph attached to an extractive study is decoration.

diagram.caption: naming leads to examining leads to acting

key_terms.meaning: Continuous examination of how your own position and presence shape the research.
Your social location conditioning access, blind spots and responses.
Letting people speak in their own terms; 'giving voice' is itself a power.
Research that gives something back to those who give time and trust.
Speaking through participants instead of carrying their words faithfully.
Whether a commitment changed a design or only appeared in text.

worked_example.title: Test one study against the five
worked_example.setup: A team plans interviews with women agricultural labourers. Their proposal has a positionality paragraph and a line on 'giving voice'.
steps: Reflexivity test: what did we change because of it? Add a journal entry after each fieldwork day.
Positionality test: which axes mattered here? Caste and institution (read as officials), so name those only.
Power test: who set the question? Record refusals as data.
Voice test: whose categories are these? State how quotations were selected.
Reciprocity test: what flowed back and when? Add a budget line and a date for a findings meeting.
worked_example.answer: Each commitment now changes the design, which is the difference between practised and decorative.

mistakes: Writing reflexivity as a closing section instead of questions asked at each stage.
Listing every identity instead of the axes that mattered in this study.
Treating a refusal to answer as missing data.
Intending reciprocity without a budget line or date.

recall.q: State the one-line test for each of the five commitments.
recall.a: Reflexivity: what did I change? Positionality: which axes mattered? Power: who set the question? Voice: whose categories? Reciprocity: what flowed back, and when?

recall.q: Why does positionality come first in the sequence?
recall.a: Without naming where you stand, reflexivity has nothing to examine.

recall.q: What does the deck say about the phrase 'giving voice'?
recall.a: It assumes people had none and re-centres the researcher as the one who grants it.

recall.q: Which two reciprocity forms are cheapest and least practised?
recall.a: Returning findings accessibly and crediting contributors by name.

recall.q: What is the honest test on your own work?
recall.a: Name one thing you did differently because of these commitments.

sections.title: Standpoint Theory
sections.big_idea: Those at the margins must understand both worlds, so they can see more of the system. **A standpoint is achieved, never automatic.**
in_plain_words: Standpoint theory holds that position shapes what can be known, and that dominated groups can give a more complete account of how a system works. It does not say all views are equal, that suffering guarantees insight, or that identity confers a standpoint. Marx's proletarian standpoint is its ancestor.

Harding's strong objectivity scrutinises the data, the question and the knower. Smith starts from the everyday and traces outward to ruling relations, and Hill Collins adds the matrix of domination and the outsider within. The hard questions remain: which standpoint, romanticising, access for outsiders. **Specify the standpoint** in your study.

key_terms.meaning: An achieved critical understanding won through reflection on shared experience of power.
Harding's idea that examining your position and assumptions adds rigour.
Smith's method of tracing how texts and rules organise everyday life.
Smith's term for the institutional relations that set categories.
Hill Collins's idea of interlocking systems of oppression.
Someone inside an institution yet never fully of it.

worked_example.title: Specify the standpoint
worked_example.setup: A proposal says research will be 'from the margins'. A reviewer asks which margins.
steps: The first hard question: which standpoint? There is no single woman's or poor person's view.
Rewrite narrowly: from the standpoint of Dalit women agricultural labourers in this district.
Check the second question: are we romanticising? Plan to test insight and avoid assuming it.
Check the third: can outsiders access it? Partially, through sustained engagement.
State the limit: this standpoint cannot speak for all women.
worked_example.answer: A specific, defensible standpoint replaces 'from the margins' and guards against essentialism.

mistakes: Reading standpoint theory as identity politics.
Assuming suffering guarantees insight.
Treating 'the margins' as one fixed perspective.
Mapping Hill Collins from race to caste without citing the South Asian literature.

recall.q: Why do those at the margins see more of the system?
recall.a: To survive they must understand their own world and that of the powerful, who need understand only their own.

recall.q: What is strong objectivity?
recall.a: Examining the researcher's location and starting assumptions as rigorously as the evidence.

recall.q: What is institutional ethnography?
recall.a: Starting from everyday experience and tracing outward to the institutional relations that organise it.

recall.q: What are the four domains of the matrix of domination?
recall.a: Structural, disciplinary, hegemonic and interpersonal.

recall.q: Name one hard question for standpoint theory.
recall.a: Any of: which standpoint, romanticising the margins, whether outsiders can access it, essentialism.

sections.title: Situated Knowledges
sections.big_idea: All knowledge is made from somewhere. **Say where**, and your claim becomes something others can check and hold accountable.
in_plain_words: Haraway's 1988 essay rejects both the god trick, a view from nowhere that claims to see everything, and pure relativism. Her answer is that partial, located perspective is the only route to objectivity, because a located view can be held accountable. Embodiment extends to instruments: surveys, satellite images and models are particular ways of seeing.

In practice, state where knowledge was produced, name what your vantage saw and could not see, and ask the same of cited work. Standpoint and situatedness are allies, and four questions work on any evidence: from where, with what instruments, for whose purpose, and what could it not see. **If you can apply one, apply this one.**

key_terms.meaning: The illusion of seeing everything from no particular place.
Knowledge produced from a specific, embodied, accountable location.
A located view; for Haraway, the only route to objective vision.
Knowledge comes from particular eyes, instruments, languages and histories.
The ability to question a claim because its origin is known.
Where the vantage point's blind spots are named.

worked_example.title: Read a national poverty estimate
worked_example.setup: A report says 'the data show' a fall in poverty. Apply the four questions.
steps: From where was it made? Which country's data, and in what setting?
With what instruments? Which survey categories defined poor?
For whose purpose? Commissioned by whom?
What could it not see? The population outside the frame.
Rewrite the claim so its location is stated, making it checkable.
worked_example.answer: The estimate becomes a located claim with a stated boundary, which a reader can weigh.

mistakes: Writing in the passive voice with no author, so a situated claim looks origin-free.
Treating a model output as the world with no stated assumptions.
Using a generic limitations section.
Treating relativism as the only alternative to a view from nowhere.

recall.q: What is the god trick?
recall.a: The illusion of seeing everything from no particular place.

recall.q: Why does partiality make accountability possible?
recall.a: A located view can be questioned about where it was made; a view from nowhere cannot.

recall.q: Name two instruments the deck calls situated.
recall.a: Any two of: a satellite image, a national survey, an administrative record, a model output.

recall.q: What do both failures share?
recall.a: They escape accountability by refusing to say from where a claim is made.

recall.q: Which of standpoint and situatedness does the deck say to apply if you can use only one?
recall.a: Situated knowledges, by stating your location.

sections.title: Intersectionality in Research
sections.big_idea: Intersectionality studies how systems of power **combine to make distinct positions**. Decide your intersections at design.
in_plain_words: Crenshaw coined the term in 1989 to describe how courts recognised race discrimination or sex discrimination but missed the combination. The image is a crossroads: the harm at the intersection is more than the sum of the roads. Adding caste as a control removes it from view, while crossing gender by caste, using interaction terms or fitting separate models shows it.

In South Asia, caste, class and gender are the usual intersections, and the data to cross them mostly exists. The reading is structural, about interlocking systems, so study the mechanism too. Report the bottom group beside the mean. **Sample for small groups at design**, and choose structurally significant intersections instead of slicing endlessly.

key_terms.meaning: Analysis of how multiple systems of power combine into distinct experiences.
Treating gender and caste disadvantage as two separate coefficients.
Splitting an overall figure to show which group is furthest behind.
A regression term testing whether an effect differs by group.
Sampling extra of a small group at design so it is visible.
Seeing intersectionality as interlocking systems as well as identity labels.

worked_example.title: Size a sample for the crossing
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. You plan a survey of 1,000 people and want to compare Dalit women with others. They are about 5% of the population.
steps: Gender by caste gives four cells in the simplest case: 2 × 2 = 4.
Proportionate sampling gives Dalit women: 1,000 × 0.05 = 50 respondents.
Suppose you need 200 in that cell to estimate it. A proportionate sample would need 200 ÷ 0.05 = 4,000 people.
The cheaper route is oversampling Dalit women at design.
Decide before collection, since the sample cannot be fixed afterwards.
worked_example.answer: A proportionate 1,000 gives 50 Dalit women. Reaching 200 needs oversampling or a 4,000 sample, decided at design.

mistakes: Reading intersectionality as a list of identity labels to collect.
Controlling for caste and then claiming the gap is explained.
Slicing a sample into cells too small to estimate.
Assuming small groups can be made visible after collection.

recall.q: What did Crenshaw's 1989 paper analyse?
recall.a: How anti-discrimination law failed Black women by recognising race or sex discrimination but not the combination.

recall.q: What is wrong with adding caste as a control?
recall.a: It removes caste from view instead of showing where the burden falls.

recall.q: Which Indian datasets already carry caste, class and religion?
recall.a: NFHS, NSS and PLFS.

recall.q: What should you report beside the mean?
recall.a: The bottom group's figure, as a standing practice.

recall.q: Which intersections does the deck say are almost always relevant in South Asia?
recall.a: Caste and gender.

sections.title: Feminist Methods
sections.big_idea: No method is feminist in itself. **The questions, the power relations and the use of findings** make research feminist.
in_plain_words: Feminist research favours qualitative methods because closed instruments cannot let people speak in their own terms. Oral history recovers what archives erased, and participatory research shifts who frames, collects, interprets and decides. Feminist quantitative work counts the uncounted, such as time use, and disaggregates relentlessly.

Feminist methodology resists a single hierarchy of evidence applied regardless of question. Trials are good for average effects, and qualitative work answers different questions. Mixed methods pair scale with mechanism, with the qualitative collected before the quantitative result is known. **State the question first, then choose the method.**

diagram.caption: any method can serve the commitments

key_terms.meaning: Recovering experience through testimony where written archives are silent.
Communities help frame, gather, interpret and use findings.
Measures unpaid work such as care and domestic labour.
Breaking figures down by group to make inequality visible.
Statistics for scale plus accounts for mechanism.
Choosing the method that suits the question and respects the people.

worked_example.title: Match the question to the method
worked_example.setup: A project has four questions. Which method fits each, using the deck's logic?
steps: 'How many women left wage work after marriage?' A figure from a survey gives scale.
'Why did they leave, and what did it cost?' A life history gives mechanism and meaning.
'Does the scheme work on average?' A trial suits an average-effects question.
'What did Partition do to women whose records were never kept?' Oral history recovers what archives erased.
Where the number and the accounts disagree, report the disagreement.
worked_example.answer: Survey, life history, trial, oral history. No method ranks above the others; fit decides.

mistakes: Assuming only qualitative methods can be feminist.
Choosing participatory methods as a signal of virtue.
Applying one evidence hierarchy before stating the question.
Collecting accounts after the quantitative result is known, so they illustrate a conclusion.

recall.q: Why can a randomised trial be feminist research?
recall.a: Because the label attaches to the practice and the questions, and the instrument does not decide it.

recall.q: What does oral history recover?
recall.a: Histories that official documents never recorded, such as women's experiences of Partition.

recall.q: What does a time-use survey show?
recall.a: Unpaid domestic and care work, which labour statistics had erased.

recall.q: What is the cost of the qualitative lean?
recall.a: Scale and comparability.

recall.q: What is the sequencing advice for mixed methods?
recall.a: Collect the qualitative material before the quantitative result is known.

sections.title: Ethics & Non-Extraction
sections.big_idea: Ethics is **a relationship** that no form can capture. Plan what flows back, anticipate harm after you leave and settle who owns the data.
in_plain_words: Institutional review is a floor. Feminist ethics also asks whether people understood and could refuse, whether anything flowed back and who controls the data. Consent is ongoing, informed, free of coercion and comprehended, which is hard when you are linked to a scheme. An ethic of care means attending to what a person needs now, stopping when someone is distressed and having referrals ready.

The extractive model arrives, collects, leaves and publishes elsewhere. The minimum correction is a date, a budget line and a commitment to return findings. Representation, harm after the interview and data ownership all need planning. **You leave the field; participants do not**, so leave a named contact who will respond.

key_terms.meaning: Arrive, collect, leave and publish elsewhere, with value flowing out.
Ethics grounded in attentiveness and responsiveness within relationships.
Agreement based on understanding use and sharing, free of coercion.
Communities' right to govern data about themselves.
How participants are portrayed in the write-up.
A written arrangement on who holds, uses and profits from data.

worked_example.title: Budget the minimum reciprocity
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A study covers 3 villages and 40 participants who each give a half day.
steps: Plan two findings meetings in the local language per village: 3 × 2 = 6 meetings.
Credit contributors by name, with consent. This costs almost nothing.
Pay fairly for time. If a day's fair rate is Rs 300 (an invented figure): 40 × 300 = 12,000 rupees.
Put a date and a budget line against each, in the proposal.
Leave a named contact and a working number.
worked_example.answer: Six meetings and Rs 12,000 (illustrative) are planned and dated, so reciprocity does not depend on goodwill.

mistakes: Treating ethics approval as proof that a study is not extractive.
Taking a thumbprint on an unexplained form as consent.
Portraying participants as passive victims or numbers.
Publishing disaggregated data that could re-identify someone in a small village.

recall.q: Why is ethics review only a floor?
recall.a: It checks that people signed and harm was avoided, but not whether the relationship is fair or anything flowed back.

recall.q: What is the structural difficulty with consent?
recall.a: Where the researcher is linked to a scheme, refusal may feel costly.

recall.q: What is the minimum correction to the extractive model?
recall.a: A date, a budget line and a commitment to return findings in a usable form.

recall.q: What is the practical test of representation?
recall.a: Whether the person would recognise themselves in your account and accept it.

recall.q: From when does the DPDP Act place duties on researchers and NGOs?

sections.title: Reflexivity & Relationships
sections.big_idea: The research encounter is **part of the data**. Record how who you are shaped what you were told.
in_plain_words: An interview is an encounter between people, and rapport, silence and discomfort are information. Insider and outsider positions each distort in a different way: insiders are told less because explanation is assumed unnecessary, and outsiders misread the unfamiliar. Most positions are in between, with insider status on some axes and outsider status on others.

Power flows in more than one direction, since gatekeepers and elites control access and narrative. Emotions in the field are signals, and easy rapport can mean a shared position and shared blind spots. Reflexivity is daily practice: a position statement before, a journal during, questions in analysis and a reflexive account in writing. **Cut any line that does not help a reader weigh the findings.**

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.sub: ask how your lens read it

diagram.caption: a daily practice across the project

key_terms.meaning: Shares group membership; has trust but takes the familiar for granted.
Needs brokers and time; may misread the unfamiliar.
Someone who controls who you meet.
Daily record of reactions, surprises and unease beside field notes.
A short methods statement on position, access and influence.
Comfort that may reflect shared position and blind spots.

worked_example.title: Name the axes that mattered
worked_example.setup: A woman researcher from an urban institution interviews rural women of a different caste about scheme access.
steps: Shared axis: gender, which may open private conversation.
Differing axes: caste, class, language and institution.
Predicted effect: she may be read as an official, so answers lean toward scheme eligibility.
Record in the journal when a respondent defers or gives a rehearsed account.
Write two sentences in the reflexive account on how this shaped what was said.
worked_example.answer: Insider on gender, outsider on caste, class and institution; the account says how that shaped answers.

mistakes: Standardising the interviewer away instead of recording the encounter.
Describing yourself simply as an insider or an outsider.
Treating the researcher as always holding all the power.
Writing the reflexive account as a confession or a claim to have overcome bias.

recall.q: Why are insiders told less?
recall.a: Explanation is assumed unnecessary, and that absence is invisible in a transcript.

recall.q: What does easy rapport often indicate?
recall.a: A shared position and shared blind spots.

recall.q: What goes in a reflexive journal?
recall.a: Your reactions, surprises and unease, alongside field notes.

recall.q: What four things belong in a reflexive account?
recall.a: Axes that mattered, how access was gained, how your presence shaped answers, and what your position obscured.

recall.q: How long does the deck say daily reflexive journaling needs?
recall.a: Ten minutes.

sections.title: Decolonial & Southern Feminisms
sections.big_idea: Southern and Dalit feminists applied standpoint thinking **to feminism itself**. Ask who is speaking for whom at every scale.
in_plain_words: By the 1980s feminists from the global South challenged a Western feminism that universalised a white, middle-class experience. Mohanty's 1984 essay showed how scholarship built a monolithic 'Third World woman' defined by lack. Her method lesson: do not treat women as one group, show agency within structure, check imported categories and refuse the rescue frame.

Indian feminist scholarship developed its own questions, and Dalit feminists pressed the same critique inside Indian feminism. The pattern repeats at every scale. Decolonising practice means citing Southern theorists as theory, building on regional scholarship, questioning imported categories, sharing the analysis stage and publishing where people can use it. **Count where your bibliography's theory comes from.**

diagram.caption: the same move at three scales

key_terms.meaning: Mohanty's term for a flattened image of Southern women as victims.
Casting Southern women as objects to be saved.
A claim of shared experience that can centre the privileged.
Critique of caste-blind mainstream Indian feminism.
Citing Southern theory, testing categories, shifting authority.
A concept that may not exist in the local setting.

worked_example.title: Audit a bibliography
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A South Asia study cites 40 works and 6 are South Asian theory.
steps: Count the South Asian theory: 6 of 40.
Share: 6 ÷ 40 = 0.15, which is 15%.
Check how they are cited: as theory or as case material?
Read the regional and Dalit feminist work directly, without relying on summaries.
Re-cite where the regional tradition made the argument first.
worked_example.answer: 15% of the bibliography is South Asian theory; the audit shows where to build on regional scholarship.

mistakes: Treating South Asian scholarship as a local application of Western theory.
Measuring an imported category without checking that it exists locally.
Publishing research about a place only behind a paywall in a language few residents speak.
Using 'sisterhood of all women' as if caste did not matter.

recall.q: What did Mohanty's 1984 essay critique?
recall.a: A monolithic image of the 'Third World woman' defined by lack against an implicit Western norm.

recall.q: What did Dalit feminists critique?
recall.a: Mainstream Indian feminism, led largely by upper-caste women, universalising its experience.

recall.q: Name two Indian feminist questions with no Western equivalent.
recall.a: Any two of: household as a site of inequality, invisible labour, personal law, Partition, caste with patriarchy.

recall.q: What does the deck say about citing Southern theorists?
recall.a: Cite them as theory, in their own right, and avoid treating them as data or context.

recall.q: What is the recurring lesson of the course?
recall.a: There is no view from nowhere, and that includes feminist views.

sections.title: Doing It & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: At each stage you choose between **reproducing power and answering back**. Ten questions and a short reading list make it practical.
in_plain_words: The five stages are question, design, fieldwork, analysis and writing. At each the default reproduces existing power, so the commitments must be applied deliberately. Pick the two stages with most discretion, usually design and writing. Answer the first five questions before design and revisit the second five at midline and write-up.

Data Feminism brings these ideas into data work, with questions about who made the data and whose reality has no category. Read primary texts, Southern and Dalit sources, and Data Feminism. Rehearse the drop-and-carry pairs. **If you carry one idea, carry this one:** name where your knowledge was made.

diagram.caption: the first five, asked before design

key_terms.meaning: A checklist answer that shows the commitment was not applied.
Repeating the during-and-after questions at midline.
D'Ignazio and Klein's 2020 book applying these ideas to data science.
The original work, read instead of a summary.
Pairs of misreadings to drop and ideas to carry.
A one-sentence question each of the five takeaways becomes.

worked_example.title: Fix a failing checklist answer
worked_example.setup: A study's pre-design answers: whose question? 'The funder's terms of reference'. Where do I stand? 'Never considered'. Which intersections? 'We will disaggregate by sex'. Who will be missing? 'The sample is representative'.
steps: Whose question: honest, so name it and decide what to add to it.
Where do I stand: write the axes that matter, such as caste, language and institution.
Intersections: add caste and class to the design and size the sample for the crossing.
Who will be missing: replace 'representative' with a named list of groups outside the frame.
Write the answers before the design is fixed.
worked_example.answer: Each failing answer becomes a design input, written before the design is fixed.

mistakes: Answering the checklist after the design, so it becomes a justification.
Reading summaries of Haraway, Harding or Crenshaw in place of one primary text.
Discarding responses that did not fit the option set.
Citing no South Asian theory in a South Asian study.

recall.q: At which stages does the deck say most practitioners have the most discretion?
recall.a: Design and writing.

recall.q: When should the first five checklist questions be answered?
recall.a: Before the design is fixed.

recall.q: What does the deck advise when respondents keep qualifying answers?
recall.a: The option set is wrong, so record the responses that did not fit.

recall.q: Name a Data Feminism principle and the question it poses.
recall.a: Consider context: what does this number not say? (Others are on the slide.)

recall.q: Which takeaway does the deck say to carry if you carry one?
recall.a: There is no view from nowhere: name where yours is from.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a reading order. Sections 1 to 3 give the definition, history and five commitments, sections 4 to 6 the three theories of knowledge, 7 to 9 the doing, and 10 and 11 the Southern critique and the checklists. **Read section 3 before any method choice**.
notes.4: Clear the commonest misconception first. Feminist research is a stance on knowledge and power, so it can be applied to irrigation policy as much as to women's work. The slide's test is useful: **did the framing of the question change?** If only the analysis changed, the lens arrived too late.
notes.5: Hold the two columns together. Feminist research keeps ordinary standards of evidence and adds a second set of questions on top: true for whom, whose question, who is missing, who benefits. Calling research a political act **describes the choices as consequential** and does not license choosing findings politically.
notes.6: Memorise the five decision points as a map of where facts get made: funder, discipline, sampling frame, researcher, and journal or client. The practical form of the argument is small. **Document these five decisions** in any study, and the resulting fact stops presenting itself as simply true.
notes.7: Ask the three questions of your own proposal: whose question, whose voice, whose benefit. Conventional work leaves all three with the researcher and funder. The third row is the one participants notice most, so **name who benefits in the proposal** and check whether reciprocity was planned or only assumed.
notes.8: See definitions as decisions. Who counts as poor, what counts as work, who heads a household and what counts as violence each decide what the state sees and who receives help. When a number moves, **ask whether the world changed or the category did**, since both happen and get confused.
notes.9: Study the paired examples. The feminist framing keeps the rate and asks why so much work goes uncounted, with the woman answering for herself instead of through the household head. Both can be rigorous. The fourth row matters: asking the woman directly is a methodological change with **large, measured effects**.
notes.10: Keep the four misreadings ready because reviewers raise them reliably. Feminist work includes statistics, meets high standards, concerns everyone's position, and makes values explicit. The last answer is the important one: Harding argues that mainstream objectivity is **too weak**, and that objectivity remains possible.
notes.12: Start from the empirical roots of the critique. Medical research on men generalised to everyone is the familiar case, and it made the argument testable: **unexamined position produces demonstrably worse findings**. The claim to neutrality was itself an unmarked position.
notes.13: Use the waves as a rough map only. The slide stresses that they are a Western shorthand that flattens other histories, since South Asian feminisms followed their own timelines. For research, the second wave mattered most because it made housework, care, sexuality and domestic violence **legitimate subjects of study**.
notes.14: Learn the slogan through its consequences. Unpaid care, intimate-partner violence and household bargaining are now mainstream topics because feminists argued that the kitchen and the bedroom were political. The argument is unfinished, and **several areas remain badly measured** because the categories predate their treatment as work.
notes.15: Treat Harding's three positions as live options that you choose between, with no ladder to climb. Feminist empiricism fixes bias with better science, standpoint theory starts from the margins, and postmodern feminism distrusts universal claims. The empiricist route is easiest to carry out, and **the standpoint route asks you to change who sets the question**.
notes.16: Feminist empiricism asks for more careful, more inclusive science, such as women in trials or an occupational code with a care category. Its strength is that it needs no philosophical agreement. Its limit is that **it cannot see bias built into the standards themselves**.
notes.17: Pay attention to the third row. A standpoint is an analytical achievement won through struggle and reflection, and belonging to a group does not confer it. That answers the commonest objection, that standpoint theory reduces to identity, so **say the distinction aloud** when the objection comes.
notes.18: Treat postmodern feminism as a source of humility with a known risk. It reminds you that 'woman' is many things, but its relativism can dissolve the political ground a movement needs. Most researchers hold the tension. Haraway, in section 5, is **the main attempt to keep the insight without the relativism**.
notes.19: Read this as a correction to the story of the field. South Asian scholarship on caste and patriarchy, the household and invisible labour developed in parallel with the Western tradition. A concrete practice follows: **cite regional scholarship as theory in its own right**, and keep case material for the data.
notes.21: Learn the five as one-line tests: what did I change, which axes mattered, who set the question, whose categories, what flowed back. They are independent, so adopting any one improves a study. **Pick the weakest of your five** for the project in front of you.
notes.22: Ask the reflexivity questions at each of the five stages, from design to writing, and let the answers change decisions. Keep a short journal entry after each fieldwork day on what surprised you and what you assumed. That journal is **the raw material of the reflexive account**.
notes.23: Use positionality as an analytic tool. A high-caste urban researcher and a local Dalit fieldworker will not get the same answers, and the table shows how each axis affects your data. Name only **the axes that mattered in this study**, and make the paragraph explain something about the data.
notes.24: Map power in both directions. The participant's levers are what to reveal, what to withhold, whether to grant access again, and silence. A refusal to answer is information, so **record it** and look at the pattern of refusals across your sample.
notes.25: Be careful with the phrase 'giving voice'. It assumes people had none, and it re-centres the researcher as the one who grants it. Say what you selected and why, and treat quotation as evidence. Where you quote, **explain how the quotation was selected**, since one vivid line from two hundred interviews is a choice.
notes.26: Read the table as a ladder of cost and practice. Returning findings and crediting contributors are cheap yet rare, so the barrier is habit and planning. **Put reciprocity in the budget and the timeline**, because an intention without a line item produces the right-hand column.
notes.27: Follow the sequence: positionality names where you stand, reflexivity examines it, and power, voice and reciprocity act on it. That explains why positionality comes first, and why voice and reciprocity are often missing: **they require acting, and noticing is easier**.
notes.28: Use the right-hand column as your standard. A positionality paragraph is decoration unless a design changed because of it. The honest test closes the slide: **name one thing you did differently** because of these commitments. If nothing comes to mind, they were recited.
notes.30: Hold the definition and the misreadings together. Standpoint theory says position shapes what can be known and the margins can see more of the system. It makes no claim that all views are equal or that identity confers insight. The third misreading **derails most discussions**, and Marx's proletarian standpoint is the ancestor.
notes.31: Use the double-vision argument: those without power must understand their own world and the powerful one, while the powerful need know only their own. It concerns position and survival, and says nothing about virtue. Test it on a case you know: **a domestic worker knows both the kitchen and the drawing room**.
notes.32: Learn Harding's reversal: mainstream objectivity is too weak because it checks the data and never the values in the question. Strong objectivity examines the knower too. For practice, add one section asking **what assumptions are built into the question and who would have asked it differently**.
notes.33: Keep the comparison table as an argument you can make to sceptics. Examining your own position claims more rigour than mainstream practice, since it scrutinises the question as well as the data. It is also harder, because it requires **describing yourself, starting from marginal lives and owning the limits**.
notes.34: Use Smith's method for bureaucratic programmes: begin with what a person's day is actually like, then trace outward to the texts and rules that shaped it. That is institutional ethnography, and it starts from the person with the programme coming second. It makes the 'relations of ruling' **visible from below**.
notes.35: Remember the matrix as interlocking systems across four levels: structural, disciplinary, hegemonic and interpersonal. The payoff is diagnostic, since it tells you where an injustice lives and so what would change it. For South Asia, **use the literature on caste and gender** directly instead of mapping it from race.
notes.36: Use the outsider-within position as a source of insight and be candid about its cost. These researchers are close enough to see an institution's workings and distant enough to question them. Research that recruits them should say the position is personally costly, and **never treat it as a free resource**.
notes.37: Treat the four hard questions as open and practise answering them. The practical one is the first: specify the standpoint, for example Dalit women agricultural labourers in this district, which is **more specific and defensible than 'from the margins'**. Guard against romanticising the margins.
notes.39: Haraway offers a path between false certainty and 'it's all just perspective'. Her idea is that acknowledging partiality is the precondition of objectivity. Read the 1988 essay if you can. The practical translation is simple: **say where knowledge was made** and the claim becomes checkable.
notes.40: Spot the god trick in reports: no author in the text, no statement of position, universal claims from one context, and models presented as the world. The device is partly stylistic. Treat 'the data show' as a prompt to ask **who produced the data, where, and with what category**.
notes.41: Read Haraway's twist carefully: a located view can be held accountable, and a view from nowhere can be questioned nowhere. The four questions in the table are the accountability check. The idea to carry is that **acknowledging limits strengthens a claim**, since it tells a reader how far to trust it.
notes.42: Place situated knowledge between two failures. The god trick claims one view is all views, and pure relativism treats all views as equally untrue. Both escape accountability by refusing to say from where a claim is made. Accountability is **the price of making a claim at all**.
notes.43: Extend embodiment to instruments. A satellite image, survey, administrative record and model are each a way of seeing built by someone for a purpose. A more productive question than whether the numbers are accurate is **what this instrument cannot see**.
notes.44: Use the four practices as a methods and limitations template. State where knowledge was produced, name what the vantage saw and could not see, and ask the same of cited work. Most limitations sections are generic, and **one that names what your vantage could not see** does the work situatedness asks for.
notes.45: Treat the two traditions as allies: both reject the view from nowhere and both make the knower part of the knowledge. Standpoint guards against erasing the marginalised, and situatedness guards against the god trick and relativism. If you can apply only one, **apply the second**, since stating your location is open to every study.
notes.46: Take the four questions into every meeting: from where was this made, with what instruments, for whose purpose, and what could it not see. They work on a World Bank projection, a poverty line or your own evaluation. They are **usable without preparation**, which is why they beat a fuller framework nobody remembers.
notes.48: Learn the origin: Crenshaw diagnosed a failure of legal categories, where courts recognised race discrimination or sex discrimination and missed the combination. The origin is legal and specific. Intersectionality was a **diagnosis of a failure in a category system** before it became a theory of identity.
notes.49: Remember the crossroads: a person at the intersection can be hit from several directions at once, and the harm exceeds the sum of the roads. In analysis, controlling for caste removes it from view while crossing by caste shows where the burden falls. **Interaction terms need samples big enough to estimate them**.
notes.50: Choose your analytic move deliberately and say which you used. Adding caste as a control is the default, and it hides an intersectional pattern while seeming to account for it. Crossing, interaction terms and separate models reveal it. A reader **cannot tell from a coefficient table** which you chose.
notes.51: Use the table to see what data you already have. Caste, class, religion, region and language are collected in NFHS, NSS and PLFS, while disability is under-measured. The gap is that these are rarely crossed and published. Where a variable is never collected, such as sexuality, **saying so is itself a finding**.
notes.52: Read the chart as an illustration of a pattern, using no real figures. An overall rate is an average of unequal lives, so a programme can improve the mean while the target group stagnates. Make it standing practice to **report the bottom group beside the mean**: one extra row changes what the table says.
notes.53: Take the structural reading seriously. Collecting identity labels is the thin version. The original point concerns interlocking systems such as caste and patriarchy. A workable proxy: **study the mechanism**, such as land tenure, a labour arrangement or a credit relationship, alongside the demographic marker.
notes.54: Decide your intersections at design and size the sample for them. Oversampling cannot be added after collection, and a sample that cannot support the crossing you need will not support it however you analyse. Define categories **with communities**, and add qualitative work to analyse the mechanism.
notes.55: Intersect with judgement. Naive slicing yields cells too small to estimate and dissolves a shared political claim. Ask which intersections matter for the power structure you study. In South Asia **caste and gender are almost always among them**, and any others should be argued for the setting.
notes.57: Remember the title claim: there is no feminist method in itself, and none that cannot be used feministically. What defines the research is the question, who decided it, how power is handled and what is done with findings. A randomised trial can qualify, and **an interview study can fail to**.
notes.58: Understand the qualitative lean as a consequence of the commitments. If people are to speak in their own terms, a closed instrument cannot deliver that, so interviews, oral history and participatory work are common. The cost is scale and comparability, a **real trade-off** that argues against neither approach.
notes.59: Use oral history where records are silent. The marginalised rarely leave written archives, and Partition testimony recovered women's experiences that the nationalist record had silenced. It brings its own duties: consent for archiving, protection of identity, and **honesty about memory as a source**.
notes.60: Follow the four steps as a shift in who decides: the community helps frame the question, co-designs what counts as data, gathers and interprets, and decides the use. Participation is slower, harder to fund and not automatically more accurate. **Choose it because the question calls for it.**
notes.61: Treat counting as feminist work. Time-use surveys and gender-disaggregated budgets are entirely quantitative and feminist. Rejecting numbers would hand the most influential form of evidence to people using the categories this course criticises. The strongest policy arguments on unpaid work in India **rest on a national statistical instrument**.
notes.62: See the questionnaire as political. India's Time Use Survey made unpaid domestic and care work visible, and what is counted can be budgeted, argued over and represented. The method is conventional, and **the choice of what to measure** is the feminist act.
notes.63: Choose the method for the question. The slide objects to a single ladder of evidence applied regardless of question, and it leaves trials alone for questions about average effects. 'Does this work on average' and 'why does it fail here' are different questions, so **state the question first**.
notes.64: Combine numbers and accounts deliberately: figures give scale, comparison and pattern, and accounts give mechanism and meaning. Sequence matters. **Collect the qualitative material before the quantitative result is known**, or the accounts become illustrations. Where the two disagree, report the disagreement.
notes.66: Treat ethics review as a floor. The right-hand column asks whether people understood and could refuse, whether the relationship is fair, whether anything flowed back and who controls the data. No committee covers these, so they depend on you. **Seek formal review even where nobody requires it**.
notes.67: Consent here is a relationship. It is ongoing, informed about later use, free of coercion and comprehended. The structural difficulty is the third row: where you are linked to a scheme, refusal feels costly. Say that participation is unconnected to any benefit and **make sure that is true first**.
notes.68: Use the ethic of care as a practical stance. Ask what this person needs now, have referral support ready, and stop an interview when someone is distressed. Never treat a person's pain as a 'rich' data point. The tradition of Gilligan, Noddings and Tronto is **a real alternative to rules-and-rights ethics**.
notes.69: Name the extractive default plainly: arrive, collect, leave and publish elsewhere, with the value flowing out. It is a harm and a poor default. The minimum correction is small: **a date, a budget line and a commitment** to return the findings in a usable form.
notes.70: Read the table as a cost ladder. Cost and substance rise together, and the cheap forms (sharing findings, recognition) are the ones most often skipped. Budget for the first two at minimum, with a date, because reciprocity that depends on **goodwill after the grant ends** does not happen.
notes.71: Check your drafts for portrayal as passive victim, exotic other or number. The 'poor rural woman' needing rescue serves the rescuer. The practical test: **would the person recognise themselves** in your account and accept it? Where you can, ask them.
notes.72: Think past the interview. Publication can expose a participant, disaggregated data can re-identify someone in a small village, and local relationships can strain after you leave. The row researchers skip is the last one: leave **a named contact and a working number** so participants can raise a problem.
notes.73: Separate the legal floor from the ethical standard. The DPDP Act sets duties on personal digital data from 13 May 2027, and the research exemption in s17(2)(b) is narrow. Feminist ethics asks who holds the data, who controls later use and who profits, so **settle these in a data-sharing agreement**.
notes.75: Treat the relationship as part of the data. Who you are changes what people say, rapport or its absence is a finding about position, and what was not said signals safety. Write **a short note after each interview** on how the encounter went; it explains a great deal at analysis.
notes.76: Compare insider and outsider by the distortion each causes. Insiders are told less because explanation seems unnecessary, and that absence is invisible in a transcript. Outsiders misread the unfamiliar. Ask **what each position is doing to your data**, since neither is simply better.
notes.77: Break the binary. You are usually an insider on some axes and an outsider on others at once, so ask on which axes you are an insider and how each shapes what you are told. A short statement naming the axes that mattered is **more informative than an account of your identity**.
notes.78: Map power in each encounter accurately. Gatekeepers control access, rehearsed accounts control the narrative, silence withholds, and local authority steers the conversation. Assuming you hold all the power misses these. The elite interview inverts the usual relation, so prepare **specific questions, documented facts and no deference**.
notes.79: Keep a record of your emotions. Discomfort may signal a boundary crossed, anger an injustice you just understood, grief how hard the content is. The least obvious row is easy rapport: it often means a shared position and shared blind spots, so **ease is itself a finding about who you can reach**.
notes.80: Run reflexivity as a daily practice: name your position before, keep a journal during, ask how your lens shaped the reading in analysis, and report the influence in writing. Ten minutes a day is enough. Reconstructing assumptions only at the writing stage gives **a plausible account that may be inaccurate**.
notes.81: Write the reflexive account as a methods statement. Include the axes that mattered, how you gained access and through whom, how your presence shaped answers and what your position obscured. Keep it to a paragraph or two, and **cut any line that does not help a reader interpret the findings**.
notes.83: Read the critique as feminism applying its own method to itself. Southern feminists challenged a Western feminism that universalised a white, middle-class experience and cast other women as objects of rescue. It came from within the movement, and it is **a standpoint argument applied reflexively**.
notes.84: Use Mohanty as a lesson in reading categories. Her 1984 essay shows how scholarship built a monolithic 'Third World woman' defined by lack against an implicit Western norm. The lesson for development research is direct: the **'beneficiary' in many programme documents is built the same way**.
notes.85: Turn Mohanty's critique into method. Treat 'women' as many groups, show agency within structure, watch imported categories and refuse the rescue frame. The practical row is the third: **check whether a category exists locally before measuring it**. Household headship, formal employment and 'the family' do not map cleanly.
notes.86: Read these as theoretical contributions in their own right. Each question arose from a specific South Asian arrangement: intra-household allocation, the formal-informal divide, personal law, Partition, and caste with patriarchy. Citing them as theory is part of decolonising practice, and the household literature is **influential internationally**.
notes.87: Read Dalit feminist critiques as the same argument one level in. Mainstream Indian feminism, led largely by upper-caste women, often universalised its own experience. Read the scholarship directly: it is a substantial body of work with its own theoretical positions, and **summaries compress it**.
notes.88: Use this slide as a three-step pattern: Western feminism speaking for the global South, elite Indian feminism for all Indian women, upper-caste women for Dalit women. The lesson nests at every scale, so **always ask who is speaking for whom**, including inside your own team.
notes.89: Treat decolonising as concrete practice: cite Southern theorists as theory, build on regional scholarship, test imported categories, share the analysis stage and publish where people can use it. The first row is measurable: **count where the theory in your bibliography comes from**.
notes.90: Notice the full circle. Standpoint and situated knowledge, applied to feminism itself, produced the Southern and Dalit critiques. The table ends with you. The test: **whose account does your study take as the general case**, and who is thereby positioned as the exception?
notes.92: Turn commitments into choices at each of the five stages. At every stage the default reproduces existing power, so the commitments must be applied deliberately. Pick the two stages where you have most discretion; for most practitioners those are **design and writing**.
notes.93: Answer these five before the design is fixed. Written afterwards they become a justification. The first failing answer, the funder's terms of reference, is honest but incomplete: **name the funder's question** and decide what to add to it. Check your answers against the failing examples in the second column.
notes.94: Revisit these five at design, midline and write-up. Watch for responses that do not fit your options: when respondents keep qualifying answers, the option set is wrong. **Record the responses that did not fit**, since they are usually the most informative material and the first thing a coding frame discards.
notes.95: Use the Data Feminism principles as questions for any dataset: who made it for whom, whose reality has no category, are the people still visible, what does the number not say, who did the work of collecting it. The book is **free to read online**.
notes.96: Pick one primary text and read it in full, in place of three summaries. All four are more readable than their reputation suggests, and Haraway is the hardest and the shortest. Summaries in circulation flatten the arguments in **the same directions**.
notes.97: Read the Southern list as the practical form of decolonising. The sources exist and are cited far less than the first list. Pair this deck with Research Ethics, Qualitative Methods and Data Literacy 101. If your bibliography on a South Asian study has no South Asian theory, **that is a finding about the study**.
notes.98: Rehearse the drop-and-carry pairs as one-sentence answers for review meetings. The last pair, that the field is a Western import, is the one that most often ends a discussion, and it can be answered on the record: **the regional tradition is substantial and independent**.
notes.99: Turn the takeaways into five questions and ask them of your own study. If you carry one, carry the second: naming where your knowledge was made is open to every study and **makes everything else checkable**.
